title: Washington Is Taking Control of AI
dek: Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia is looking less like a resignation and more like Washington firing him. As the lame-duck Congress returns, China hawks and newly empowered Democrats are using the scandal to push export controls, haul executives in to testify, and rebalance power between Washington and the most important company in AI.

oneIdea.headline: Washington fired Jensen, and that's the opening salvo of a new era of AI politics.
oneIdea.summary: Set aside the conspiracy theories. Even without any coordinated campaign, the Jensen affair marks a shift: Democrats are asserting power over foreign policy and over powerful private-market actors, and China hawks are ascendant. Three chip-control bills now look likely to pass, the hearings will stretch into 2027, and the real question is no longer whether Alice Huang was a spy. It's whether Nvidia knowingly let its chips reach China. Markets may move on quickly. The political consequences are only beginning.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: Little clinical relevance; a pricing point
items.body: This edition is American trade politics and changes nothing in the consulting room. One economist's point is worth noting: if the United States builds data centres more slowly, the price of AI services there stays high. NHS tools mostly run on American models, so that feeds through to what suppliers charge us. Zitron's allegations concern Nvidia's accounts, not service prices.

items.title: Chinese models and patient data
items.body: If the reports are right that leading Chinese models were trained on smuggled hardware, they are more capable and cheaper than their official story suggested, and some vendors will be tempted to use them. For anything touching patient data the questions are unchanged: where is it processed, under whose law, and has the DPIA covered it. Cheap is not a reason.

items.title: Who the company answers to
items.body: A congressman said Nvidia should put national security first. NLW reads that as the state taking control; Zitron as the law catching up. The NHS has lived with this tension for decades: suppliers of clinical systems answer to shareholders, and we rely on contracts and regulators to align them with patients. It is worth reading those contracts with that in mind.

the_other_side.source: Premium: The Hater's Guide To Megaspeed
the_other_side.text: Zitron, in a paid piece published the same day of which only the opening is free to read, does not see Washington seizing control of a private company. He sees overdue attention to conduct he says was reported for more than a year and ignored. He alleges Megaspeed is one part of a sprawling smuggling operation, and writes that Nvidia has "repeatedly and unashamedly profited from breaking the law". He repeats a short seller's claim that over a fifth of last fiscal year's revenue may have come from China-bound sales. These are his allegations; the free section does not discuss the chip-control bills.

the_truth_beneath.text: The variable both men orbit is whether Nvidia knew its chips were reaching China. Both accept as fact that restricted chips got there in quantity, that Megaspeed was a large customer under investigation, and that Huang will be questioned under oath. The empirical question is what Nvidia's leadership knew and how much revenue was involved; the observable is the testimony, the documents Congress has asked to be preserved, and any Justice Department charges. The residue is worldview: whether this is the state asserting itself over a powerful company, or a company finally being held to existing law. For Whittemore to be vindicated, the lasting result must be political, with new chip laws and long hearings while markets move on. For Zitron, investigators must show knowing diversion on a scale that changes Nvidia's accounts. Both are polemicists with incentives: Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype. The signal is that both now say smuggling, not espionage, is the real issue. Watch Huang's testimony before Thanksgiving.

headlines.headline: Washington fired Jensen
headlines.summary: Calling it a resignation undersells what happened. Even without any coordinated campaign, this looks like the opening salvo of a new period: Democrats asserting power over foreign policy and over powerful private-market actors, with China hawks increasingly ascendant.

headlines.headline: Nvidia must now change its corporate practices and appoint leadership that makes national security its top priority.
headlines.attribution: Rep. John Moolenaar, Chairman of the House Select Committee on China
headlines.summary: The House Select Committee on China's statement called Huang's exit a "firing." NLW points to the subtext: the idea that a private company's top priority should be national security rather than its fiduciary duty to shareholders shows the power struggle that has now opened up.

headlines.headline: The scandal vaults chip controls to the top of the lame-duck agenda
headlines.summary: Export controls were already expected to ride on the must-pass NDAA. Now Democrats plan to push for even tougher restrictions. One aide's message to Republicans who were nervous about crossing the White House: if they don't deal now, Democrats write the next version.

headlines.headline: A hawkish consensus forms, with White House help
headlines.summary: Speaker Mike Johnson sees a "developing consensus." Leader Thune calls passage a high probability. House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast says the week has "one hundred percent boosted" the chances of all three chip bills, adding that they're getting "direct assistance from the White House."

headlines.headline: The case for selling China older chips: machine guns vs. muskets
headlines.summary: Gavin Baker argues that selling China a few generations behind (H100s while the US runs Vera Rubin) meant scaling laws would keep American labs structurally ahead. In this view, a full ban pushes China down its own hardware path and gives it a real chance to catch up.

headlines.headline: The pro-sales camp never made its best argument
headlines.summary: Jensen and other advocates almost never publicly framed selling worse chips as a way to keep China dependent on an inferior supply. Their pitch was about whether we should be competing with China at all, which was a much weaker argument.

headlines.headline: The hawks' answer: we tried arming them, let's try the other way
headlines.summary: Dmitri Alperovitch replies that the current approach produced Chinese models less than nine months behind the US frontier, so now we can test denying all compute. He concedes it won't be a clean experiment, since so much Nvidia hardware has already been smuggled in.

headlines.headline: The simpler argument is going to win
headlines.summary: Whoever is right on strategy, "it's been a leaky sieve, so let's give them nothing" needs no knowledge of scaling laws. It will resonate far more than the technical case. Meanwhile Beijing has been steering its companies toward domestic chips like Huawei's either way.

headlines.headline: The Jensen affair is reviving a Cold War mentality
headlines.summary: The Telegraph compared it to the Klaus Fuchs scandal of the 1940s, which broke the Western nuclear monopoly. CSIS's Scott Kennedy expects Democrats to nudge China policy in a more hawkish direction, constrained by executive-branch latitude and China's growing leverage.

headlines.headline: Why slowing US data centers makes chip denial more urgent
headlines.summary: Natixis economist Gary Ng warns that a slower US build-out keeps American token prices high, which opens the door for China to export cheap inference backed by abundant electricity. If Democrats slow data center construction, cutting off China's chips becomes the way to do it without surrendering the lead.

headlines.headline: Jensen heads to Congress under oath
headlines.summary: Bloomberg reports Huang agreed to a closed-door, transcribed House hearing before Thanksgiving. The China Select Committee is still threatening a subpoena, and Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott wants a separate hearing on export controls.

headlines.headline: Jensen Huang's decision to resign from NVIDIA does not absolve him… They still owe Congress answers.
headlines.attribution: Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Senate Banking Committee ranking member
headlines.summary: NLW reads the subtext: this isn't about the affairs (a second one was reported, and it's now a footnote), or even mainly about Alice Huang. It's about whether Nvidia knowingly contravened export controls, and what Jensen knew about Megaspeed giving Chinese companies access to its chips.

headlines.headline: Lutnick is the official most in the line of fire
headlines.summary: Reports say Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick slow-rolled export-control enforcement all year, which rivals frame as defying presidential orders. Insiders are split on whether he'll be fired, since the President was too directly involved for an easy scapegoat. One official called it "a complete and utter disaster."

headlines.headline: Expect this to stretch well into 2027
headlines.summary: Senators Warren and Coons, the incoming chairs of Banking and Foreign Affairs once Democrats take Congress in January, asked the administration to preserve all documents on Nvidia's chip exports, Jensen's relationship with Alice Huang, and what intelligence suspected about her.

headlines.headline: The spy narrative starts to wobble
headlines.summary: CNN reports the intelligence on Alice Huang doesn't yet prove she was spying. ODNI officials called the characterization "over-torqued," and the AG says no conclusions have been reached. Former AI czar David Sacks declared the narrative "collapsing" and called for an investigation into the leak of the classified memo.

headlines.headline: Whether she was a spy will matter less and less
headlines.summary: Some will read the whole affair as a China-fearing hatchet job on a powerful private company. NLW expects the hearings and investigations to center on a different question: did Jensen know about, or help facilitate, chip smuggling into China?

headlines.headline: The smuggling story keeps getting bigger
headlines.summary: Bloomberg saw documentation of chips moving from Singapore to a data center in China. The Information reports that companies linked to Alice Huang invested in DeepSeek and promised it a steady stream of Blackwells. The DOJ is probing her ties to Super Micro, whose co-founder was charged with smuggling in March.

headlines.headline: Model weights carry a fingerprint of the GPU that trained them
headlines.summary: Former OpenAI researcher Will DePue says initial weight layouts depend on the exact GPU and seed, and traces survive training. After searching 6 trillion combinations, he says six Chinese models, including DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3 and MiniMax-M3, were initialized on Blackwell systems. He says senior OpenAI and Anthropic researchers independently verified the result.

headlines.headline: If true, the "fraction of the compute" story falls apart
headlines.summary: Stephen Lubka's read: Chinese labs weren't building competitive models on scraps. They used latest-gen hardware plus distillation of top models to run about six months behind at lower cost.

headlines.headline: Nvidia staff rally for Jensen as Colette Kress takes the reins
headlines.summary: A memorial sits outside Nvidia's entrance, and an internal post urging the board to reconsider has 1,600 comments, most backing Jensen's return. CFO Colette Kress, at Nvidia since 2013, is interim CEO. Reports say Jensen tended to "steamroll her" and dismissed her as a reporting CFO.

headlines.headline: The CFO who pushed back on the $250B guarantee
headlines.summary: The Information says Kress resisted Nvidia's more extravagant underwriting, including a proposed $250 billion guarantee backstopping 8 gigawatts of compute for OpenAI. It was pared back to $100 billion for the first half of the build-out. She's not ultra-conservative, but she's unlikely to stick her neck out like Jensen did.

headlines.headline: Nvidia is the central bank of AI, and it might tighten credit
headlines.summary: Nvidia has invested in dozens of startups and co-signs NeoCloud leases. A pullback could hit like banks pulling credit in a downturn. Its $500 billion financing vehicle with six PE giants, which guarantees GPU residual value on up to 25% of deal size, has signed no deals, and partners want a bigger backstop.

headlines.headline: Markets move on: "If Nvidia is out of the way, who wins?"
headlines.summary: After falling 20% in three days, Nvidia found a bottom on the resignation and traded slightly higher Thursday, a reminder that investors hate uncertainty most. The Nasdaq is up 4.8% on the week, and analysts see Broadcom, Intel and startups filling the cracks Nvidia leaves.

headlines.headline: OpenAI quietly backs all three chip-control bills
headlines.summary: Anthropic has long supported export controls, but OpenAI stayed noncommittal until this week. Politico reports it privately told congressional offices it supports all three bills. Sen. Jim Banks calls it a "generational opportunity" to close every pathway China uses to get chips.

headlines.headline: The story will turn forward fast, but the implications have barely begun
headlines.summary: Markets want to know who benefits, politicians want to pass legislation, and the Anthropic IPO next week will pull attention forward. Still, NLW expects the consequences of this moment to keep unfolding long after the news cycle moves on.
